claims.text: Configurational entropy-induced stabilization of the solid solution primarily governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Configurational entropy suppresses surface premelting in these nanoparticles.
Configurational entropy raises the nanoparticle melting point above the weighted average for the constituent metals.
Random atomic distribution and local chemical disorder reduce the driving force for phase separation.
Random atomic distribution and local chemical disorder reduce surface disordering relative to less chemically complex or monometallic nanoparticles.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are single-phase solid solutions with a random atomic distribution.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution.
Solid-solution stabilization reduces segregation of surface atoms before bulk melting.
Solid-solution stabilization reduces disordering of surface atoms before bulk melting.
Reduced pre-melting segregation and surface disorder delay premelting and raise the melting point.
The premelting onset of the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will be higher than the weighted-average premelting baseline from constituent-metal nanoparticles.
The melting point of the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will be higher than the weighted-average melting point of constituent-metal nanoparticles.
Surface disordering will be suppressed before melting.
Phase separation will be suppressed before melting.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles between 10 and 50 nm under an inert atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to larger, phase-segregated, or reactively heated particles.
There is a lack of direct prior studies on Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is inferred from findings on bulk high-entropy alloys and bimetallic nanoparticles.
Premelting or melting at or below the weighted-average constituent-metal baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Significant surface disordering or phase segregation before melting would falsify the hypothesis.
